title: The queen exiled
hook: Maharani Jind Kaur is separated from her son and sent away

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi, and your line, lost at a table. Today, the treaties reach the palace, and a mother.

A carriage waits in a palace courtyard in Lahore. The woman being taken to it has ruled the Punjab in her son's name. She has argued with ministers, faced down the army's councils, and spoken her mind to British officials. Now there are guards at her side, and the boy Maharaja is not coming with her. Somewhere in the palace behind her is her son. She is being sent away from him.
screen: `A CARRIAGE IN THE COURTYARD.` → `GUARDS AT HER SIDE.` → `HER SON STAYS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: After the war, a new agreement put the Punjab's government in the hands of a council of the court's chiefs and ministers, guided by a British Resident at Lahore. Maharani Jind Kaur, who had been regent, was set aside with a pension. Her son stayed on the throne, but she no longer had any say in how he was raised or how his kingdom was run. The British Resident came to believe she was plotting against the new order, and histories record accusations of a plot against British officials. She denied it, and the evidence is still argued over. Whatever the truth, the decision was made. She was taken from Lahore to the fort at Sheikhupura, some miles from the city, while the boy was kept at the palace. Later she was sent much further, out of the Punjab altogether. Histories record her protests, sharp and grieving, against being parted from her child. She asked for her son, and she wasn't given him. The boy, too young to choose anything, stayed among officials and tutors. Sikh memory calls her Rani Jindan and holds her up as a mother and a queen who would not bow quietly, even when she lost. Some British writers of the time painted her as dangerous; Sikh tellings remember her courage. Both views appear in the histories, and today's story belongs to her grief. A crown can be taken by treaty. Taking a child from his mother is a different kind of loss.
screen: `SET ASIDE WITH A PENSION.` · `A CHARGE OF PLOTTING.` · `SHE ASKED FOR HER SON.` · `RANI JINDAN, WHO WOULD NOT BOW.` · then, large: `MOTHER AND SON APART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind any mother who is far from her child today: across a border, in a hospital, in a prison, separated by work, by war, by a court's decision, or by death. You don't need her name; just hold her in mind, and the child too, and breathe slowly for both of them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, holding them together for a moment.
Maharani, great queen, the title by which Jind Kaur is remembered: set aside, accused, and sent away from Lahore, while her son, the boy Maharaja, stayed behind.
Your line: mother and son apart. Some losses no treaty can name. Day nine hundred thirty-six.
